opus-5.5.text:
I think compute scarcity is one of the most underrated factors here. People tend to imagine that once a model can do a task, it just gets deployed everywhere at once. But in practice, labs and their customers face a real allocation problem: there's only so much inference compute available at any given time, and it has to go where it earns the most per unit of compute.

So the first jobs to get automated in a serious way probably won't be the ones that are easiest for AI in some abstract sense. They'll be the ones where the ratio of economic value to compute cost is highest. That favors work done by highly paid people, where even a modest productivity gain is worth a lot. Software engineering is the obvious example: it's well paid, the output is digital, it's easy to verify whether code runs, and labs have a direct incentive because automating their own engineering speeds up their own research. You see the same logic in parts of finance, law, and research-adjacent knowledge work.

By contrast, a lot of lower-wage cognitive work, like basic customer service, might technically be within reach, but if running a capable agent costs a meaningful fraction of what you'd pay a human, the margin isn't compelling while compute is tight. Those jobs get automated more as inference costs fall and hardware supply expands.

There's also a time-horizon effect. Tasks that require an agent to operate coherently over hours or days burn a lot of tokens, so long-horizon work is expensive even when it's feasible. Early on, you'd expect automation to concentrate on high-value tasks that can be broken into shorter chunks.

So my rough picture is that compute acts like a filter that releases automation in order of value density. As the stock of compute grows, and it's growing very fast, that filter loosens, and you move down the wage distribution and into more compute-hungry tasks. But the ordering in the meantime is driven much more by economics than by which tasks feel "hard" to humans.

r001.rationale: The response says automation favors highly paid work when value per unit of compute is high, but it does not state the criterion’s equal deployment-cost condition.

r002.rationale: It says a job may be technically automatable yet uneconomical when the AI agent’s cost is a meaningful fraction of the human wage.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare worldwide compute with the compute equivalent of all human brains.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key thing to realize is that compute is going to be the binding constraint for a long time, and that changes the question from "what can AI do" to "what is AI worth spending compute on." Those are very different questions.

If you have a model that can do a task, but running it costs more than paying a human to do the same thing, you're not going to automate that task. So labs are going to look at where the ratio of economic value to compute cost is highest. That points you toward work where a relatively small amount of tokens produces a lot of value. Software engineering is the obvious case, and it's not a coincidence that's where everyone is focused. A few thousand tokens of good code can be worth a lot, and you can verify whether it works, so you don't waste compute on long rollouts that go nowhere.

The flip side is that tasks which need enormous amounts of context, long horizons, lots of back and forth with the physical world or with other people, those are compute-expensive per unit of value. Even if the capability is there in principle, you might not deploy it widely because the inference bill doesn't make sense. Something like a hospital administrator's job might technically be automatable before it's economically automatable.

There's also a second-order effect, which is that labs themselves are compute-constrained in their own operations. So they'll prioritize automating the things that make them more compute-efficient. AI research, running experiments, writing training code. If you can turn compute into better algorithms, that compounds. Automating a customer service job doesn't compound in the same way.

So my rough picture is: first the high-value, easily verifiable, short-horizon cognitive work, especially the work the labs do themselves. Then as compute gets cheaper, you move down the value-per-token curve into things that are messier and lower margin. And I'd expect the gap between "demonstrated in a benchmark" and "actually displacing workers" to be larger than people assume, precisely because of this cost structure.

r001.rationale: The response says labs prioritize work with the highest value relative to compute cost, but does not state the condition that all jobs have the same deployment cost or that labs would then prioritize the highest-compensated jobs.

r002.rationale: It says a hospital administrator’s job might be technically automatable but not economically automatable because the inference bill does not make sense.

r003.rationale: The response does not estimate worldwide compute relative to the compute equivalent of all human brains.

astra-6.text:
I think limited compute pushes labs to be selective about what they automate. It’s not enough that an AI can do a job; it has to do it cheaply enough that using the compute for that job makes sense compared with other things you could use it for.

So you’d expect them to focus on tasks where the value produced per unit of compute is high. That could be parts of software engineering or research, where a relatively small amount of work can be very valuable. A task might be technically easier to automate, but if human labor is cheap and the model needs a lot of inference to do it reliably, it might come later.

AI research itself is particularly interesting for the labs because automating it could help them make better models or use their existing compute more efficiently. That gives it a value beyond just saving on salaries. But I’d expect this to happen at the level of particular tasks first, rather than entire jobs. You automate the parts where the economics work and leave humans doing the rest.

r001.rationale: The response says labs favor high value per unit of compute, but does not state the equal deployment cost condition or that labs would prioritize the highest-compensated jobs.

r002.rationale: It says a task may come later if human labor is cheap and the model needs substantial inference to do it reliably, making automation uneconomical despite its potential value.

r003.rationale: The response makes no estimate comparing worldwide compute with the compute equivalent of all human brains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think limited compute means you have to distinguish between what an AI system can do and what it’s actually economical to use it for. You might have a system that can automate a job, but if doing that takes a huge amount of inference compute, it may still be cheaper to employ a human.

So the first jobs you automate won’t necessarily be the easiest ones. They’ll be the ones where the value produced per unit of compute is highest. A task that takes an expensive professional several hours but takes the model a few minutes is an attractive target. A task that requires the model to run continuously, while replacing relatively inexpensive labor, is less attractive—even if the model is perfectly capable of doing it.

For AI labs, research and engineering are especially interesting because automating those tasks could help them develop better systems or use their existing compute more efficiently. That gives the work an additional payoff. But there’s still an opportunity cost: compute used by an automated researcher can’t simultaneously serve customers or train the next model. So I’d expect selective automation of particularly valuable tasks before wholesale replacement of entire occupations.

r001.rationale: It prioritizes tasks with the highest value per unit of compute, but does not state that equal deployment costs would make labs prioritize the highest-compensated jobs.

r002.rationale: It says an AI-capable job may still be cheaper to perform with a human when the task takes a huge amount of inference compute.

r003.rationale: It makes no estimate comparing worldwide compute with the compute equivalent of all human brains.
